Simulacra feels like a proper sequel to Sara is Missing, which is the viral free-to-play phone sleuthing game. The visuals are upgraded, the acting is better and the characters are more numerous and more involved. This time around it's more like a story with and about characters, rather than a story with a character here or there. Overall, the game's absolutely worth your time.

This game is so much fun. I really liked how, even though I had kinda figured out the big reveal at the end, there was enough of a twist to it that I still didn't see it coming fully. The multiple endings gives it great replay value, which is always appreciated. 

It has what is called "Begin+", which makes it where, instead of taking time for the other characters to type their texts in, you can receive them rapidfire, which I found quite nice. That made my second playthrough take about an hour, while my first playthrough took about 3.5 hours.

The best part in my opinion, is that it has a fantastic horror vibe to it without being so suspenseful that I have to take a break. I really love a horror game that gets my heart racing without making it to where I have to detach myself, and this game did that perfectly.

开发者的想法值得肯定：通过探索陌生人的手机，来解开最终迷题。毕竟，如今，手机对我们每个人都很重要。我们都隐隐约约担心手机信息安全问题。而且，这个游戏相对来说，也并不貴。这是我推荐这个游戏的原因。
但就游戏本身而言，这个游戏比较无聊。里面的文字排序迷题，和图片迷题很无聊，对话（包括各式信息，视频中的独白等）让我昏昏欲睡。这些对话太老生常谈了，太无聊了，根本没有勾勒出有性格、让人想了解的人物形象。而对话却又恰恰是这个游戏中非常重要的一部分……

I decided to recommend it based on the innovative idea that players are required to explore a stranger's phone. It is an attractive idea, as we all care about our phones so much today. Data leaking has raised worries about data security. Plus, the price of this game is relatively low. 
However, the game is boring. The puzzles (word and pic puzzles) are humdrum, and the dialogue (messages or videos) makes me sleepy. That dialogue, which plays a crucial role in the game, has not reflected or created exciting characters—only cliche.

[h1] A game for people with questionable morals. [/h1]

The game itself is decent, a very good idea is coupled with relatively cheap jump scares, blah blah blah.

But after finishing the game & looking through the guides for the various endings, I'm just like, "Why is the moral compass of the developers so incredibly fucked up??!"

Decide for yourselves (moderate spoilers ahead):

1. Wanna get the best ending? [spoiler]  - You have to lie to Anna's closest friend from start to finish, fool her into thinking you're Anna and even trick her into a relationship without Anna's consent. [/spoiler]

2. Wanna get an okay-ish ending? [spoiler] - You have to trust a very, VERY untrustworthy registered sex offender and send him Anna's selfies and personal emails at his request and without Anna's consent. [/spoiler]

3. Wanna get the worst ending where everyone dies? [spoiler] - You have to be an honest and decent person, protect Anna's privacy as much as possible, don't get involved with shady people and tell the truth to Anna's friends.
 [/spoiler]

Just let this sink for a moment. 
What is the game trying to teach you with this? 
I got the worst ending and the game blames me for [spoiler] not trusting Taylor. [/spoiler] How so?! My common sense says NO.
[spoiler] No, I don't feel guilty at all for not trusting a sex offender on a dating site, who would ONLY give me valuable information about RESCUING A MISSING PERSON, if I send him photos of that person without her consent in exchange. Especially since Taylor keeps making flirty jokes about this very person. He just comes across as perverted, horny and a sensationalist, and not like someone who seriously cares about Anna's well-being. Even Anna's cheating ex-boyfriend was more trustworthy than Taylor. [/spoiler]

Even in real life I would not trust such a person and would also not recommend it to anyone. The game teaches you exactly the opposite of how to behave.

I want to be kind to this game and for the right person, I would still recommend it. But I don't think SIMULACRA quite pulls it all off. I like the social media sleuth type games (e.g. A Normal Lost Phone.) And the horror twist on this one isn't even that bad if you don't mind breaking the whole simulationist vibe of it.

But there's quality issues. Acting and voiceover ranges from straight-faced to hammy and cartoony and it's not really clear which flavor is intended. There's also *a lot* of spelling and grammar errors that kind of break the sense of immersion. And worst of all, advancing the plot in many cases requires taking actions that the player might have a very good reason not to perform. If I suspect a character of harming the owner of this phone, why should I tell them everything I dig up from social media? Make it make sense.

Quite engaging visual novel using already seen by many setting of text quests. For me this kind of gameplay is not as shallow as it seems and does provide somewhat new experience, although I did have an experience of playing text quests or even writing them by myself way back then.

The atmosphere of typical detective storyline intersecting with personal relationships of a missing person the role of which we are playing in the process of dealing with all those unreal mystic-like happenings adds up a lot with its base gameplay.

Of course it’s not just a novel, but a horror too. And these specific elements don’t exactly work all of the time, though there are a few good examples, but mostly I got scared by sudden calls from a cop during my leisure-time reading of backed up messages. When talking about good examples, breaking the 4th wall is one of them - when you getting the choice of what’d you prefer, ‘A flying head or a headless body behind you’, I got little chills down my spine because regardless of what you chose, the following would sound like ‘Your hair smells nice’ or ‘Can I touch your hair?’, which, combined with the general atmosphere, is quite creepy and gets you tense a little (especially if there’s a whole ass room behind you).

Otherwise it’s somewhat exciting to play through this game simply because its main idea works very well and keeps you interested, though I won’t tell you an exact reasoning for this - play it yourself to get the hang of it.

Nevertheless, I’d like to add on to my positive thoughts a bit of dark sides.
Despite having a bunch of answer options during every possible dialogue, their consequences consist of several plot peculiarities:

1) Whether you get Taylor's trust or not

2) Will Ashley find out that her friend is missing

Well, that’s all. As you can see, there's not much variety here. Only these two options would subsequently affect the outcome you get - more precisely speaking, ending. You either lose everyone because you didn’t meet the requirements or save everyone instead because you dealt with it otherwise.

That’s quite shallow so to speak. It’s not a kinetic novel as most of them tend to struggle with, too straightforward and not to hard to understand either.
Considering the concept which this title has, I get a strong feeling that there could’ve been much more endings than we have as a result.

Also, referring to achievements, I’d like to blabber a bit more about it too.
Recalling that there’s not much variety here, going through your second playthrough for a ordinary click-clack to get a few achievement is an unbearable struggle that only messes up your perception of the game. Simulacra does not even allow you to watch videos simultaneously because of its ugly fullscreen resolution that you cannot change during the game.

As a conclusion, I did like it plot-wise, and maybe sometime later would consider playing its sequel. But when it comes to achievements, it’s not worth it - they are ruining your first impressions and forcing you to acquaint with its low-variety gameplay. Yeah, you can talk to people on Tinder, deal with other people struggles, sure, but it does not affect your main storyline and is present here only to give you achievements.

I’d say it’s good enough, but don’t ever hunt for achievements here.
